title: The First Certified AI Agents in Legal: Harvey Achieves AIUC-1
author: Harvey Team

dom.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility

st.t: Professional tasks: Partial credit overstates complete success
st.an: The source endorses independent, product-level scrutiny rather than vendor self-attestation, but redirects evaluation toward agent security, safety and reliability certification. It does not establish task-specific legal quality, complete-task success or production competence—the cluster’s central concerns—and its trust claim therefore extends beyond the evidence described.
qs: Self-attestation isn't enough anymore, and it shouldn't be.

"Harvey is the first legal AI company to be certified against AIUC-1, and they earned it the hard way - independent, adversarial technical testing of the actual product, not a paper review."  ### What AIUC-1 Certifies

st.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s caution that adoption or vendor assurances alone do not establish trustworthy, durable legal-AI infrastructure. It presents independent adversarial certification as an additional assurance mechanism while acknowledging that security and trust remain continuous deployment obligations, not solved outcomes.
qs: Self-attestation isn't enough anymore, and it shouldn't be.
"Security and trust aren't a single milestone, they're a continuous commitment," said Joshua McKibben, Harvey's Head of Trust.

kp.k: Harvey reports first legal AI agent certification
kp.d: In this 2026 company announcement, Harvey reports that its agentic platform achieved AIUC-1 certification through Schellman, described as the first accredited AIUC-1 certification body. Harvey claims first-mover status among legal and professional services companies. These are company-reported certification claims rather than a separately presented auditor's report.
qs: Today, we're proud to announce that Harvey's agentic platform has achieved AIUC-1 certification, making Harvey the first legal and professional services company to meet the industry's standard for AI agent security, safety, and reliability.
The certification was conducted by Schellman, the first accredited AIUC-1 certification body.

kp.k: Consequential legal AI adoption demands independent assurance
kp.d: Harvey argues that legal teams adopting AI for consequential work need independent evidence of testing and validation rather than vendor self-attestation. Harvey's Head of Trust, Joshua McKibben, frames certification as an independent technical answer to enterprise security teams' concerns about responsible agent behaviour under pressure.
qs: As legal teams adopt AI into their most consequential work, they're asking hard questions: How was this system tested? Who validated it? What happens when it fails? Self-attestation isn't enough anymore, and it shouldn't be.
AIUC-1 gives our customers an independent, technical answer to the question every enterprise security team is asking about AI agents today: can we trust this system to act responsibly under pressure?

kp.k: Harvey reports testing with zero critical failures
kp.d: The company states that AIUC-1 requires independent adversarial technical testing of its model and agentic platform. It reports evaluation through more than 3,000 unique tests against a taxonomy spanning 86 risk categories and 73 attack categories, including hallucination, tool misuse, data leakage and adversarial manipulation, with zero critical failures. The stated result concerns critical failures in this evaluation, not a claim that all possible errors were eliminated.
qs: Certification requires independent, adversarial technical testing of our model and agentic platform, not just policy documents and paper reviews.
AIUC-1's taxonomy spans 86 risk categories and 73 attack categories, covering hallucination, tool misuse, data leakage, and adversarial manipulation.
Harvey was independently evaluated against this taxonomy through more than 3,000 unique tests, and passed with zero critical failures.

kp.k: Agent assurance spans six domains and recurring reviews
kp.d: Harvey describes AIUC-1 as covering six domains and aligning with existing enterprise frameworks, including ISO 42001, the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, OWASP and MITRE ATLAS. The standard reportedly drew input from 200+ Fortune 500 CISOs and security leaders and is refreshed quarterly. Certification involves technical testing at least quarterly and annual operational-control reviews, positioning assurance as ongoing rather than one-time.
qs: AIUC-1 was built with input from 200+ Fortune 500 CISOs and security leaders across Microsoft, Google Cloud, Meta, Visa, Fidelity, and more, and it's refreshed quarterly to keep pace with how quickly AI risk evolves.

The standard evaluates AI systems across six domains: Data & Privacy, Security, Safety, Reliability, Accountability, and Society, and it's aligned to the frameworks enterprise security teams already rely on, including ISO 42001, the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, OWASP, and MITRE ATLAS.
Certification is not a one-time badge: technical testing is conducted at least quarterly and operational controls are reviewed annually.

kp.k: Product testing complements AI governance certification
kp.d: Harvey distinguishes ISO 42001 certification, which it says it achieved earlier in 2026, from AIUC-1 technical evaluation. It characterises the former as validating governance, oversight and risk management, while the latter stress-tests product behaviour such as hallucination, cross-session data leakage and responses to adversarial prompts. The company argues that enterprise legal and security teams need both management-system assurance and independently tested technical performance.
qs: We achieved ISO 42001 certification earlier this year, validating the governance systems, oversight processes, and risk management practices behind how we build and deploy AI.
It doesn't independently stress-test whether a model will hallucinate under pressure, leak data across a session, or comply with an adversarial prompt.
AIUC-1 closes that gap: where ISO 42001 audits the management system, AIUC-1 puts the product itself through adversarial, technical evaluation.
Together, they give enterprise legal and security teams a fuller picture: governance that's certified, and technical performance that's independently tested for both safety and security.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Harvey Team claims that adoption of AI for consequential legal work is increasing the need for independent technical assurance, and positions Harvey’s AIUC-1 certification as a response.
pts.d: The company describes itself as the first legal and professional services company to achieve AIUC-1 certification. Its central claim concerns assurance for legal AI adoption, rather than changes to legal employment, pricing or productivity. Harvey Team argues that product-level adversarial testing complements governance certification and gives enterprise buyers a fuller basis for assessing safety and security. Harvey’s Head of Trust, Joshua McKibben, characterizes the certification as independent support for trusting the system under pressure.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source offers company-reported independent certification and adversarial test results as its principal evidence.
pts.d: Harvey Team names Schellman as the certification body and reports more than 3,000 unique tests with zero critical failures against a taxonomy spanning 86 risk categories and 73 attack categories. It identifies hallucination, tool misuse, data leakage and adversarial manipulation as covered risks. The article also invokes existing SOC 2 and ISO credentials, input from enterprise security leaders, and alignment with other frameworks. It links to methodology and trust resources but does not reproduce individual test results, define critical failure, or report legal-task accuracy or client outcomes. The reported absence of critical failures is not presented as a measured zero hallucination rate.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Certification is announced as a current achievement in the 2026 source, with continuing testing and review rather than a one-time assurance.
pts.d: The announcement uses 'Today' without supplying a specific calendar date in the provided text. ISO 42001 certification is described as having occurred earlier the same year. Harvey Team states that the standard is refreshed quarterly, technical testing occurs at least quarterly, and operational controls are reviewed annually. The result concerns the evaluated model and agentic platform against the stated taxonomy. Future-facing language commits to continuing independent validation as capabilities, regulation and expectations evolve; it supplies no forecast date for broader legal-market transformation.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed beneficiaries are law firms, in-house legal teams and enterprise security teams evaluating AI for sensitive legal work.
pts.d: Harvey Team presents certification as additional assurance for provider-side law firms and buyer-side corporate legal departments using Harvey, and as a technical basis for enterprise security teams’ trust assessments. It also advocates high assurance standards for legal AI companies generally. The article does not identify effects on particular lawyer seniority groups, staffing structures, fees, access to justice or public legal-service outcomes.
